54-082.r: Revolutionary bodies → Abhinav Bharat and Anushilan Samiti. United Indian Patriotic Association (Sir Syed Ahmed Khan, Raja Shiv Prasad, 1888) opposed Congress, not revolutionary.

54-083.r: Doctrine of 'Passive Resistance' → propounded by Aurobindo Ghosh in his newspaper 'Vande Mataram'; Indians to keep protesting until the British left.

54-084.r: Both correct: Subhash Chandra Bose quit as Congress President and formed the Forward Bloc (3 May 1939); Bhagat Singh was a founder member of HSRA (Delhi, 1928).

54-085.r: Kakori martyrs' jails → Ram Prasad Bismil: Gorakhpur; Rajendra Lahiri: Gonda; Roshan Singh: Allahabad (Prayagraj); Ashfaq Ullah: Faizabad (Ayodhya).

54-086.r: Pt. Ram Prasad Bismil (main accused, Kakori case) → hanged in Gorakhpur jail on 19 December 1927.

54-088.r: Gopinath Saha → tried to kill Calcutta Police Commissioner Charles Tegart (12 January 1924) but shot Ernest Day by mistake; hanged March 1924.

54-089.r: Bina Das → fired at the English Governor while receiving her degree at convocation (February 1932). Shanti Ghosh and Suniti Chaudhary shot a district magistrate (December 1931).
54-089.t: Don't mix Bina Das (convocation) with Shanti Ghosh–Suniti Chaudhary (magistrate).

54-090.r: "Criticism and independent thought are the two characteristics of a revolutionary" → Bhagat Singh.

54-091.r: Bal Gangadhar Tilak → started Lathi Club, Hindu Akhada, Ganapati Mahotsava and Shivaji Mahotsava.

54-092.r: True: Bhagat Singh founded Naujawan Bharat Sabha (March 1926). Others wrong: Anushilan Samiti → P. Mitra, Pulin Das; HRA (1924) → Sachindra Sanyal, Bismil; HSRA → Chandra Shekhar Azad.

55-001.r: Indian Home Rule Society → founded February 1905 in London by Shyamji Krishna Verma; also India House hostel and monthly 'The Indian Sociologist' (January 1905).

55-006.r: Lala Har Dayal (revolutionary scholar) → got a post in California in 1911 to teach Indian philosophy and Sanskrit.
55-006.c: Har Dayal lectured on Indian philosophy and Sanskrit at Stanford University, California; the book wrongly places Stanford in Berkeley, and the question says University of California. He is still the answer.

55-007.r: Ghadar Party → founded 1913 at San Francisco as 'Hindustan Association of the Pacific Coast' (Sohan Singh Bhakna); Lala Hardayal its founder member and torchbearer; named after paper 'Ghadar'.

55-012.r: First Chairman of the Ghadar Party (1913, USA and Canada) → Sohan Singh Bhakna; key members Lala Hardayal, Kartar Singh Sarabha, Rash Behari Bose.
55-012.t: Hardayal = torchbearer/leader; Sohan Singh Bhakna = first Chairman (President).

55-013.r: Only Rash Behari Bose was active in the Ghadar Party; Barindra Kumar Ghosh → Alipore Bomb case; Jogesh Chandra Chatterjee → Kakori case.

55-014.r: Khudiram Bose → not in Ghadar Party. Ghadar Party (21 April 1913, USA; HQ San Francisco) → Hardayal, Sohan Singh Bhakna (President), Pt. Ramchandra, Barkatullah, Rash Behari Bose.

55-018.r: Ghadar → revolutionary association of expatriate Indians (Canada, America), headquarters San Francisco, founded 21 April 1913 to free India.
55-018.t: Not Singapore, Berlin or Tashkent: Ghadar HQ = San Francisco.

55-020.r: Ghadar revolutionaries in World War I → based in San Francisco, in the western USA (North America).
55-020.c: Ambiguous: book takes (c) West America, but admits (b) North America is right by continent.

55-021.r: Ghadar Revolution → sparked by the outbreak of World War I (1914): 'England's distress is India's opportunity'.
55-021.t: Not the Komagata Maru incident; the trigger was the start of World War I.

55-022.r: Raja Mahendra Pratap → set up first Provisional Government of India at Kabul, Afghanistan (1915), as President; Maulavi Barakatullah its Prime Minister; recognised by Germany and Russia.

55-025.r: Bhikaiji Rustam Cama → 'Mother of Indian Revolution'; Parsi; first to hoist the Indian flag on foreign soil, International Socialist Congress, Stuttgart (Germany), 1907.

55-026.r: Madam Bhikaji Cama → Parsi (born 24 September 1861), Dadabhai Naoroji's private secretary; unfurled the flag at Stuttgart in 1907, not Paris (statement 1 wrong).
55-026.t: Flag hoisted at Stuttgart, Germany, not Paris.

55-031.r: Hanged for killing British officers in England → Madan Lal Dhingra (shot Curzon Wyllie, 1 July 1909) and Udham Singh (killed Michael O'Dwyer, London, March 1940).
55-031.h: Udham Singh avenged Jallianwala: O'Dwyer had backed the massacre.

55-034.r: Madam Bhikaji Cama, M. Barkatullah, V.V.S. Iyer and M.N. Roy → all prominent revolutionaries working for India's freedom from different foreign countries.

55-035.r: V.D. Savarkar → extended Abhinav Bharat Society to London in 1906, when he went there to study law.

55-036.r: Kamagatamaru → Japanese ship chartered by Gurdit Singh; sailed 1914 with 376 Indians to Vancouver, Canada, but they were refused entry.

55-038.r: Kamagatamaru episode → Baba Gurdit Singh, the Punjabi businessman who chartered the ship.
55-038.c: Option misprints Gurdit Singh as 'Gurdip Singh' (book notes the error).

55-040.r: Order: Ghadar Party (21 April 1913) → Indian Independence Committee, Berlin (WWI; renamed after 1915) → Central Assembly bomb (8 April 1929) → Chittagong Raid (18 April 1930).

55-041.r: Headquarters: Swadesh Sevak Home → Vancouver; United India House → Seattle; Yugantar Ashram → San Francisco; INA (Azad Hind Fauj) → Rangoon.

55-042.r: Indian Independence League → Rash Behari Bose (Tokyo conference, 28-30 March 1942; structured at Bangkok Convention, June 1942).
55-042.t: Rash Behari Bose (Japan) founded it, not Subhash Bose.

56-001.r: Last of these: Partition of Bengal (1905). Earlier: Permanent Settlement (Cornwallis, 1793); Subsidiary Alliance (Wellesley); annexation policy/Doctrine of Lapse (Dalhousie, 1848-56).

56-002.r: Anti-partition (Swadeshi) movement → began 7 August 1905 at Calcutta Town Hall. Partition announced 20 July 1905; came into effect 16 October 1905.
56-002.h: July announce → August protest → October partition.

56-006.r: Bengal Partition → resolution signed 19 July 1905, announced 20 July 1905; BPSC accepted 19 July.

56-007.r: Lord Curzon (Viceroy, 1899-1905) → partition of Bengal announced 20 July 1905, effective 16 October 1905; annulled at Delhi Durbar, 1911.

56-010.r: Sir Andrew Fraser → Lieutenant Governor of Bengal (1903-1908) during the Partition; actively helped frame it.

56-011.r: Surendranath Banerjee → led the agitation against the partition of Bengal (1905).

56-012.r: Surendra Nath Banerjee on Bengal Partition → "The partition announcement fell like a bomb shell" (Curzon's tenure).

56-013.r: R.N. Tagore → critic of the Swadeshi movement; pleaded for better East–West understanding; attacked it in his essay 'The Cult of the Chakra' (September 1925).

56-014.r: Krishna Kumar Mitra (Brahmo leader) → first suggested boycott of British goods in Bengal, in his weekly 'Sanjibani' (13 July 1905).

56-015.r: Boycott of British goods → adopted as national policy at the Calcutta Town Hall meeting, 7 August 1905 (Swadeshi Movement launched).

56-016.r: Abanindranath Tagore → painted 'Bharat Mata' (1905, Swadeshi Movement): four-armed goddess in a saffron sari, symbol of the nation.

56-017.r: Partition of Bengal → main motive: weaken growing Bengali nationalism (Bengal = nerve-centre of nationalism); Curzon called it mere administrative readjustment.
56-017.t: Official excuse was administrative convenience; real aim was to weaken nationalism.

56-018.r: Anti-partition programmes → Boycott, Swadeshi and National Education. Non-cooperation was not among them.

56-019.r: Swadeshi and Boycott → first adopted as methods of struggle in the agitation against the Partition of Bengal (effective 16 October 1905).

56-020.r: Swadeshi and Boycott → first used against the Partition of Bengal; Swadeshi Movement formally began 7 August 1905 with the Boycott resolution at Calcutta Town Hall.

56-022.r: Both correct, II explains I: 7 August → National Handloom Day, marking the Swadeshi Movement launched on 7 August 1905.

56-023.r: Swadeshi Movement → immediate cause: Lord Curzon's Partition of Bengal; championed by Aurobindo, Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal, Lajpat Rai; Moderates opposed spreading it.

56-025.r: Partition of Bengal annulled → 1911, by King George V at Delhi Durbar (12 December 1911); capital moved from Calcutta to Delhi; Bihar and Orissa separated.

56-029.r: Swadeshi leaders: Madras → Chidambaram Pillai; Delhi → Syed Haider Raja; Bombay/Pune → Tilak; Punjab → Ajit Singh, Lala Lajpat Rai.

56-031.r: Swadeshi Movement 1905 → farmers and Muslims mostly stayed away; women took active part.
56-031.t: Women were very active; it was farmers and Muslims who were largely unaffected.

56-032.r: Vande Mataram → became theme song of the national movement during the Swadeshi Movement; 16 October 1905 was a day of mourning with rakhis tied.

56-033.r: Not correct: Liyakat Hussain led Barisal's Muslim peasants (it was Ashwini Kumar Dutta). True: Bengal National College (1906), Aurobindo principal; Tagore's Atmasakti for village regeneration.

56-034.r: Not correct: Swadeshi limited to Bengal (Lajpat Rai, Tilak, Aurobindo spread it countrywide). True: some Muslims joined; women active; Bengal farmers unaffected except Barisal.

56-035.r: Both true: Swadeshi Movement revived indigenous artisan crafts and industries; National Council of Education was set up as part of it.

56-036.r: H.W. Nevinson (British journalist) → linked with Swadeshi Movement; toured India four months reporting for Manchester Guardian, Glasgow Herald, Daily Chronicle.

56-037.r: Abanindranath Tagore (with E.B. Havell) → founded 'Indian Society of Oriental Art' to revive ancient Indian art; exponent of Swadeshi values in art.
56-037.t: Not Nand Lal Bose or Amrita Shergill.

57-001.r: Gopal Krishna Gokhale (born 9 May 1866, Ratnagiri) → graduate at 18, Sudharak editor, Congress President at 39; Gandhi regarded him as master; protégé of Ranade.

57-002.r: Gopal Krishna Gokhale → presided over the Benaras session of INC, 1905; founded Servants of India Society the same year.

57-004.r: Calcutta session 1906 → presided over by Dadabhai Naoroji, chosen by Moderates to stop an Extremist takeover and a split.

57-005.r: Calcutta INC session 1906 → flag of Swaraj unfurled by its President Dadabhai Naoroji.

57-006.r: Swaraj resolution → taken up at Benaras (1905), fully passed at Calcutta (1906); aim: self-rule, with boycott, Swadeshi and national education.
57-006.c: No answer printed; explanation points to 'to secure self-rule' (b).

57-007.r: Swaraj as national demand → first made by Dadabhai Naoroji in his presidential address, Calcutta session, 1906.

57-008.r: 'Swaraj' first uttered in INC → Calcutta session, December 1906; Naoroji: goal is self-government like the United Kingdom.
57-008.t: Not Benaras 1905 or Surat 1907: 'Swaraj' was first declared at Calcutta 1906.

57-009.r: First to use 'Swaraj' → Dayanand Saraswati (per explanation); among options, Bal Gangadhar Tilak ('Swaraj is my birthright, I shall have it').
57-009.c: Explanation says Dayanand Saraswati first used the word; Tilak is only the closest option.

57-010.r: Dadabhai Naoroji → 'Grand Old Man of India'; first Indian elected to House of Commons (1892, Liberal, Central Finsbury); INC President 1886, 1893, 1906.
hi: Grand Old Man of India (भारत के वयोवृद्ध पुरुष)

57-013.r: Not correct: Naoroji won a British Parliament seat as Conservative (he was Liberal Party). True: 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India'; Gujarati professor, University College London.

57-014.r: Not correct: Naoroji presided INC four times; it was three (1886, 1893, 1906). True: Elphinstone College professor; MP 1892; Gujarati journal 'Rast Goftar'.
